final.summary: Recommended: fused. Peak 90th pct core temp 37.87 °C (limit 38.0), tightest margin 0.12 °C, 56% of priority-weighted work done.
reasons: **Heat safety is right at the limit.** Even on the hottest-running crew members, body temperature is expected to stay just under the safety line (37.87 °C vs. a 38.0 °C limit). That's only about a tenth of a degree of wiggle room, so a hotter-than-forecast day, missed water breaks, or extra effort could push someone over. Watch for heat stress closely and be ready to pause work.

**We're giving up work to stay safe.** This plan gets a bit more than half (56%) of the most important work done. The rest is held back to keep everyone out of danger, and Sam, who is new and not used to the heat yet, is kept off the heaviest jobs during the hottest parts of the day.

**The other options aren't really better.** The "balanced" plan gets the same amount done and runs slightly hotter. Doing the trenching first thing in the cool morning (and moving shop work to another time) also gets the same amount done and runs slightly cooler, so it's worth considering if it's easy to arrange. Either way, the difference is small, and no option gets more work done safely.
*Note: the description of the morning-trenching option was cut off, so I didn't say exactly when the shop work would move to. Please confirm before sharing.*

Hard safety rules:
- Every worker's 90th percentile core temperature must stay below 38.0 °C all shift. Harder work, sun and high WBGT heat people up; 30-min shade rests cool them down.
- Breaks: at most 3 work slots in a row, then a 'rest' slot; at most 2 in a row if any of those slots has WBGT >= 30.0 °C.
- No outdoor tasks during hazards that stop outdoor work. After lightning, outdoor work stays stopped for 30 more minutes.
- Workers who are not acclimatized never do very_heavy tasks when WBGT >= 28.0 °C.
Validity: one entry per slot per worker; off-site workers rest; skills and allowed slots must match.
